reading.body:
DFW17 publishes 100,000 square feet of technical space and no IT load figure in megawatts. Because no power figure is published, this site cannot rank the campus among the 13 Texas facilities that do publish megawatts, and any translation of floor area into rack count or accelerator count would require assuming both power density and a power figure, making the result too speculative to state. What the floor area does establish is that this is a substantial, purpose-built facility, not a small edge node, but its compute ceiling relative to AI workloads remains unquantified from published data alone.

The four certifications define the compliance envelope. PCI DSS qualifies the campus to host payment-card data under industry security standards. ISO 27001 qualifies it to host workloads requiring a certified information security management system. ISO 9001 certifies the operator's quality management processes for the facility. LEED certifies that the building meets a recognized standard for energy and environmental design. None of these certifications speak directly to AI training density or high-performance compute readiness, though ISO 27001 is commonly required by enterprise and government AI tenants with data-governance obligations.

Texas has 133 mapped data center facilities, of which only 13 publish a megawatt figure, totaling 389 MW of published IT capacity across those 13. DFW17 is not among those 13, so it does not contribute to that published total and cannot be ranked within it. Richardson sits within the broader Dallas-Fort Worth metro, which concentrates a large share of Texas data center capacity, but how much of the state's actual capacity DFW17 represents is not determinable from published specifications.
